analysis.one_liner: Gives Medicare enrollees a government-endorsed drug discount card plus a high-threshold catastrophic drug benefit run by private companies.
analysis.headline: Introduced in July 2002, the bill was sent to the Senate Finance Committee and died there without a hearing or vote when the Congress ended in January 2003.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would let Medicare beneficiaries voluntarily enroll in drug discount card plans run by private companies — pharmacy benefit managers, insurers, and pharmacy systems — that the Health and Human Services Secretary would endorse. Enrollees would get negotiated discounted prices on prescriptions and, once their yearly out-of-pocket drug costs passed a tiered threshold, Medicare would pay at least 90 percent of further drug costs. The card would cost $25 a year, waived for people with incomes under twice the poverty line. Medicare, not the private plans, would carry the financial risk for the catastrophic benefit.
analysis.who_benefits: Medicare beneficiaries without drug coverage would gain discounted drug prices and a catastrophic backstop — the biggest help going to low-income seniors, whose enrollment fee would be waived and whose out-of-pocket drug costs would stop at $1,500 a year. Private pharmacy benefit managers, insurers, and pharmacy companies would also gain, winning Medicare contracts to administer the cards and collect administrative fees.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Uninsured Medicare seniors, plus PBMs and insurers

how_it_helps.text: Enrollees would get access to negotiated discounted prices on prescriptions through a standardized government-endorsed card, with discounts from manufacturer negotiations required to be passed on to beneficiaries [S2] [S3].

Once out-of-pocket drug costs pass income-tiered thresholds — $1,500 a year for people under twice the poverty line, $3,500 for those between 200 and 400 percent of poverty — Medicare would cover the rest, paying the private plan at least 90 percent of those drug costs [S3].
The $25 annual enrollment fee would be waived for beneficiaries with incomes below 200 percent of the poverty line, and plans could not deny enrollment based on health status [S3].

The bill includes enrollee protections: guaranteed access to retail pharmacies, disclosed formularies and prices, grievance and appeal procedures, and a cap on cost-sharing for catastrophic-benefit enrollees at 10 percent of a drug's cost [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Taxpayers, through the Medicare Supplementary Medical Insurance Trust Fund, would pay the catastrophic benefit — at least 90 percent of covered drug costs for beneficiaries past their threshold — plus negotiated administrative fees to the private plans. Middle- and higher-income seniors would still pay large amounts out of pocket: $3,500 to $5,500 a year before help kicks in, depending on income.
analysis.who_pays_short: Medicare trust fund and middle-income seniors

drawbacks.text: The catastrophic thresholds are high. A middle-income senior would pay $3,500 out of pocket before getting help, and a senior between 400 and 600 percent of poverty would pay up to $5,500 — for many beneficiaries the card would deliver only modest discounts, not real coverage [S3].

There is no government negotiation with drug manufacturers. Discounts depend on whatever the private plans can negotiate voluntarily, and the bill explicitly exempts those negotiated prices from the Medicaid 'best price' rules that otherwise push manufacturers toward lower prices [S3].

The design routes public dollars through private middlemen: pharmacy benefit managers and insurers would bid for contracts, collect administrative fees, and control the formularies that decide which drugs are covered, while the government bears the catastrophic financial risk [S3].

Beneficiaries would have to show their federal tax returns to the private plan as proof of income to qualify for fee waivers and the catastrophic benefit, with repayment plus interest and penalties if the government later found an overpayment [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill offers real help where drug costs hurt most — low-income seniors would pay no fee and stop at $1,500 a year out of pocket — but for the majority of seniors the benefit is a discount card with help only after spending $3,500 to $5,500 out of pocket. The trade-off for that modest help is structurally significant: it would make private intermediaries the permanent channel for a public drug benefit, without Medicare using its buying power to negotiate prices directly, and without the transparency of a traditional government-administered benefit. Weaker, more expensive per dollar of aid, and less accountable than a comprehensive Medicare drug benefit — but more than the nothing seniors had in 2002.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced and referred to the Senate Finance Committee on July 16, 2002, and the committee never took it up before the 107th Congress ended on January 3, 2003.

narrative.text: Sen. Chuck Hagel introduced the bill on July 16, 2002, with five Senate Republicans joining as original cosponsors, and it was read twice and referred to the Committee on Finance [S3] [S5].
Six of 49 Senate Republicans signed on as cosponsors; no Democrat did [S4].
The Senate Finance Committee took no further action — no hearing, markup, or vote is recorded — and the bill died when the 107th Congress ended on January 3, 2003 [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: With the bill dead, pharmacy benefit managers, insurers, and drug manufacturers kept the status quo: no government-endorsed drug card program, and no public lever over prescription drug prices. Medicare seniors without drug coverage gained nothing and kept paying full retail prices.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Private drug-benefit middlemen; seniors got nothing

for.name: Chuck Hagel
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Medicare Rx Drug Discount and Security Act of 2002 and led its six Republican cosponsors.

for.name: 6 of 49 Senate Republicans
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, including original cosponsors Sens. Ensign, Lugar, Gramm, and Inhofe.

against.name: Senate Finance Committee
against.role: Referring committee (chaired by Sen. Max Baucus, D)
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on referral and never scheduled a hearing, markup, or vote before the Congress ended.

sides.party_line_note: All six sponsors and cosponsors were Senate Republicans and no vote was ever recorded; the bill died in committee during a period when Democrats favored a comprehensive government drug benefit and Republicans favored privately administered discount-card approaches.

industries.note: The bill lists PBMs first among eligible entities that would win Medicare contracts to run the discount cards and administer the catastrophic benefit, collecting negotiated administrative fees while the government bears the financial risk. Their revenue would come from public money, and they would control the formularies that determine what beneficiaries can get.

industries.industry: Health insurers and Medicare Advantage (Medicare+Choice) plans
industries.note: Insurers, Medigap issuers, and Medicare+Choice organizations would be eligible contractors for the government-endorsed drug plans, locking private insurers in as the delivery channel for a public benefit. The bill also rewrites Medigap rules so supplemental policies complement rather than duplicate the new plan, steering beneficiaries toward the contractor plans.

The bill sets no government price negotiation with manufacturers and explicitly exempts the negotiated card prices from Medicaid 'best price' rules, so manufacturers keep pricing power and discounts remain whatever private plans can obtain voluntarily.

Plans must include enough retail (non-mail-order) pharmacies for convenient access, guaranteeing network participation, but the plans would also squeeze pharmacy margins through negotiated discount prices.
